title: Paragraphs out of a PDF
problem: Our office copies paragraphs out of UN PDFs by hand. Can a tool turn a General Comment into a clean list of numbered paragraphs we can cite and reuse, and show me where it may have got things wrong?
facilitator_brief: The file is the raw text of CESCR General comment No. 27 as a PDF converter produced it, page by page, with a reference (paragraph count, footnote count, first words of each paragraph). The tool must check itself against the reference, flag the paragraphs where footnote text may sit, and let us take the paragraphs away as a dataset, in JSON and Markdown. Footnotes are not separated.
notes:
The problem, as I read it: an office copies paragraphs out of UN PDFs by hand and wants a tool that splits a document into its numbered paragraphs and, just as important, shows where it may have gone wrong. The facilitator sets the standard: check the result against the reference, and make every repair visible. The data is one document, CESCR General comment No. 27, as 20 pages of raw converter output, plus a reference block with the paragraph count, the footnote count and the first six words of each paragraph.

 The overview: 20 records, one per page, two fields, `page` and `text`; the top-level `count` is the string "20". The reference says 90 paragraphs, 141 footnotes, adopted 26 September 2025.  Page 1 shows the converter's habits at once. A paragraph number stands alone on its line ("1.", a line break, then "A clean, healthy…"); a section heading is split into "I.", a blank line and "Introduction"; footnote references are glued to the word before them ("waste.2") or set off by a space ("”. 3"); the footnote block at the foot of the page opens with a bare "1" on its own line, then the text, while the next footnotes read "2 Summary for policymakers…".  Page 2 opens with the header "E/C.12/GC/27" and the rest of paragraph 2, so paragraphs cross pages and the pages must be joined before the text is split. Its footnotes held a surprise: footnote 6 reads "A/42/427, p. 24." with no number, and a bare "6" turns up at the very end of the page, next to the page number.

 Counting: 88 lines are a number and a full stop alone.  Allowing any whitespace after the stop gives 90, the document's count,  and the two extra are paragraphs 23 and 87, whose number and text share a line ("23. The full realization…"). A rule for one form alone misses two or finds two.  Bare numbers on a line: 51, of three kinds: the page number in the footer (2 to 20), the first footnote on each page, and displaced footnote numbers like that "6". The footer comes in two orders, "page, GE code" and "GE code, page".  The last page ends with paragraph 90, footnotes 139 to 141 and the footer, nothing after.  Lines that start with a number and a space: 110; one is "6 November 2025" on the cover, the rest are footnotes.  No lettered sub-paragraphs "(a)": the paragraphs are plain prose, 43 to 254 words each.

I then ran these rules in a short script of my own. Dropping each page's header line, footer lines and footnote block, joining the rest and splitting at the paragraph numbers gives exactly 90 paragraphs, numbered 1 to 90 without a gap, and all 90 first six words match the reference once curly quotes and spacing are normalised. Footnotes are another matter: 129 start with their number, the other 12 lost it to the page foot, and the first footnote on each page is a bare number on a line of its own. A rule that follows the numbers has to repair all of that, and one missed number stops it on every page that follows; on 3 and 4 November, builds that tried lost the count, left footnote text inside paragraphs, or returned no app at all. So this version does the simple part by rule and flags the rest: a line inside a paragraph that is a bare number, or starts with a number, a space and a capital letter or a UN symbol, marks its paragraph as one where footnote text may sit; on this file that is 20 of 90, the paragraph at the foot of each page. A paragraph start always has a full stop after its number, so the two never mix. Separating the footnotes is left out of this exercise. Two more traps: 20 unlabelled headings such as "Right to work (art. 6)" and "Children" stand on the line just before a paragraph number and are glued to the end of the previous paragraph unless a rule catches them; and the labelled headings wrap ("III." has a two-line title). Sixteen paragraphs span a page break.

Then the shelf.  A search on PDF cleaning found nothing on the subject; the shelf is about presenting results, not converters.  A search on quality assurance led to the Analysis Function's page on testing code.  Accessible tables: four pages, the Analysis Function's first.  Citing UN documents: the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's answer.  The testing page gave the check panel its shape: tests that tell a story, "given this data, having run this code, we expect this output", and a new test for every bug found, which here means a named check for every repair the script makes.  The clear-language page: short sentences, explain a specialist term the first time, "must" for a requirement.  The tables page: right-aligned numbers, a title that states the message, the source under the table, no footnotes in data cells.  A search on working with AI assistants brought back the testing page and the Claude Code best practices, whose fifth point is the same lesson: give the machine a check that returns pass or fail.  The Library's page lists what a citation carries, the symbol first and the paragraph as the pinpoint; the citation form became a question.

Trade-offs. The script repairs only the damage I found, names each repair on screen and guesses nothing. The reference is the yardstick, not the truth: the app shows its own count next to the document's and never adjusts a result to match. No model calls; nothing leaves the browser. Footnotes are flagged, not separated. The five questions are the office's choices, not mine: headings, what to do with the lines that look like footnotes, the files to download, citation form, line breaks.

options.label: Section column
options.description: Each paragraph gets the heading it sits under, in a table column and in the exports; headings never appear inside paragraph text.

A closed "Headings found: n" box above the table lists them, so none can hide inside a paragraph.
`paragraph` (its number), `section` and `part` (the nearest heading and the roman-numbered section above it)
Each paragraph's `section` is the most recent heading before it and `part` the most recent roman-numbered heading.

options.label: Heading rows
options.description: Headings appear as their own grey rows in the table and as records in the exports, in document order, so the result reads like the document's table of contents.

fragments.text: One row per paragraph or heading, in document order: No. | Kind | Page | First line | Check. Headings are rows of their own, grey, bold and unnumbered, with "heading" in the Kind column for screen readers, so the table reads like the document's table of contents and a reader sees where each heading was found.

`kind` ("paragraph" or "heading", in document order), `paragraph` (the number; null for a heading, whose `citation` and `first_words_match` are null too), and for a heading `label` and `level` (2 or 3)
Headings are records of their own in document order, with `label` and `level` (roman-numbered or lettered: 2, unlabelled: 3).

questions.question: This version does not separate the footnotes. What should the app do with lines inside a paragraph that look like footnote text?

options.label: Flag, keep text
options.description: The paragraph text stays exactly as found; the lines that look like footnotes are highlighted and their paragraph is listed under Flagged paragraphs on tab 01, so nothing is cut on a guess.

fragments.text: One row per flagged paragraph: Paragraph | Page | Suspect lines | Why ("starts with a number and a space", "bare number", "paragraph over 300 words"). Clicking a row opens the paragraph on tab 02, with the suspect lines highlighted. A note above the table: "This version does not separate footnotes from paragraphs. It shows where footnote text may sit, so you know which paragraphs to check against the PDF. "
- **Suspect lines stay in the text.** They remain part of their paragraph's `text` and `text_raw`; the expanded paragraph on tab 02 highlights them.
- **Suspect lines.** n suspect lines on n pages, in n paragraphs; none is removed.

options.label: Flag, set aside
options.description: Lines that look like footnotes are taken out of the paragraph text and listed under Flagged paragraphs on tab 01, each logged as a repair: the text is cleaner, but a wrong guess cuts real text.

fragments.text: One row per flagged paragraph: Paragraph | Page | Lines set aside | Why ("starts with a number and a space", "bare number", "paragraph over 300 words"). Clicking a row shows the lines set aside, in full, with their page and the paragraph they came from, so a reader can put a line back by hand. A note above the table: "This version does not separate footnotes. It sets aside the lines that look like footnote text and lists them here; check them against the PDF."

- **Suspect lines are set aside.** They are removed from the paragraph's `text`, kept in `set_aside` with their page, and logged as "line set aside as possible footnote text"; `text_raw` keeps the paragraph with them, and the CSV has both.
- **Lines set aside.** n lines from n pages; every one is listed, and the paragraph count and first words are computed after setting them aside.

questions.question: Which files should the office be able to download?

options.label: JSON and Markdown
options.description: Two files: JSON for further processing and Markdown for reading and for working with a model; both carry the document's metadata.

fragments.text: Two buttons: **Download JSON** and **Download Markdown**.

options.label: Add CSV
options.description: The same two files plus a CSV for Excel, one row per record with the JSON's fields.

fragments.text: Three buttons: **Download JSON**, **Download Markdown** and **Download CSV**. The CSV has one row per record with the JSON's fields as columns, UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, every field double-quoted with inner quotes doubled, CRLF line ends, so Excel opens it.

questions.question: How should each paragraph be cited in the table and the exports?

options.label: Symbol and paragraph
options.description: The short form used in UN practice: the document symbol, then "para." and the number, as in "E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12".

fragments.text: and a **Copy citation** button that copies "`symbol`, para. n" ("E/C.12/GC/27, para. 12") and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the `citation` field of every export.
- **Citation** = `symbol` + ", para. " + the paragraph number, with `symbol` read from `WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`, never typed in.

options.label: Full reference
options.description: Everything the UN Library recommends: title, symbol, adoption date, paragraph, the UN link and the date you accessed it.

fragments.text: and a **Copy citation** button that copies the full reference, "Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, `title`, `symbol` (adopted `reference.adopted`), para. n, `doc_url` (accessed today's date)", and shows "Copied" for two seconds; the same string is the `citation` field of every export, and the header says which style is applied.

- **Citation** is assembled from fields, never typed in: `title`, `symbol` and `doc_url` from `WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`, `reference.adopted`, the paragraph number, and the access date from `new Date()` as day, month name, year. Every export also carries `adopted` and `accessed` as fields of their own.

questions.question: Should a paragraph be one block of text, or keep the PDF's line breaks?

options.label: One block
options.description: The converter's line breaks are replaced by single spaces, so a paragraph pastes into a document as one paragraph.

fragments.text: The expanded paragraph is one block of running text; a "Show the PDF's lines" toggle under it reveals the same text with the converter's line breaks and the page number where each page began, so the join can be checked.

- **Paragraph text** = the paragraph's lines joined with a single space, double spaces collapsed, trimmed. No line in the file ends with a hyphen, so no hyphen joining is done; the app counts such lines anyway and reports the number. `text_lines` keeps the original lines for the toggle and the export field `text_lines` (lines separated by " | ").

options.label: Keep breaks
options.description: The lines stay as the PDF had them, so a reader can compare against the original line by line; the CSV cell holds the breaks too.

fragments.text: The expanded paragraph keeps the converter's line breaks (a wrapping `<pre>`-like block) with a thin rule and the page number where a new page began, so a reader can compare line by line with the PDF; a "Copy as one paragraph" button gives the joined form for pasting.

- **Paragraph text** keeps the converter's lines, separated by a newline; the CSV cell holds the newlines inside its quotes (RFC 4180 allows it; Excel and LibreOffice read it). The joined form, lines joined with a single space and double spaces collapsed, is computed for the first-words check and the copy button. No line in the file ends with a hyphen; the app counts such lines anyway and reports the number in the check panel.

plan_base:
# Paragraphs out of a PDF: the numbered paragraphs of a General Comment, from a PDF converter's text, checked against the reference

## Context

The user works in an office that quotes UN documents and copies each paragraph out of the PDF by hand, removing the footnote numbers and page headers that come with it. A PDF converter copies in a second but damages the text: it breaks a paragraph across two pages, adds page headers, footers and date stamps, leaves the footnotes at the foot of each page with the paragraph text, and loses some footnote numbers. This app turns the converter's raw text of one document, `WORKSHOP_DATA.pdf_text`, into numbered paragraphs with the heading each sits under, compares the result with the document's own reference, flags the pages where footnote text may sit inside a paragraph, and lets the office take the paragraphs away as a dataset. Footnotes are not separated in this version. The pages are `records` (`page`, `text`); the yardstick is `reference` (`paragraphs`, `footnotes`, `adopted`, `first_words`); `title`, `symbol`, `doc_url` and `source` describe the document; nothing is typed in by hand.

## What I found in the data

These numbers are from the file I examined; the app computes its own.

- 20 pages, `text` filled on every page, 2,800 to 4,300 characters each; `count` is the string "20". `reference.paragraphs` 90, `reference.footnotes` 141; `reference.first_words` keyed by the paragraph number as a string.
- **Header.** The first line of every page is the document symbol.
- **Footer.** The last lines of a page are, in varying order, the page number alone on a line (pages 2 to 20) and the job code "GE.25-15926"; page 1 has "GE.25-15926 (E)" and a date stamp "051125 061125" instead. On 12 pages a third bare number sits in the footer: a footnote number the converter displaced.
- **Paragraph numbers.** 88 of 90 stand alone on their line ("1." then the text on the next line); 2 (paragraphs 23 and 87) share the line with their text. A rule for one form alone misses the other.
- **Headings.** Roman-numbered sections ("I.", a blank line, "Introduction") and lettered subsections ("A.") whose title can wrap over two lines; and 20 unlabelled headings ("Right to work (art. 6)", "Children") on the line or two lines just before a paragraph number, so a naive split glues them to the previous paragraph; the one before paragraph 73 wraps over two lines.
- **Footnotes.** Each page's footnotes sit at the foot, before the footer: the first is a bare number on its own line, a blank line, then the text; the others start with their number and a space ("7 E/2003/22…"). Every page has footnotes, so the paragraph that runs at the foot of each page carries footnote text unless the footnotes are separated: 20 of 90 paragraphs here. Builds that tried to separate them lost the count after the first missing number, so this version flags them and leaves them in place.
- **Footnote marks in the text.** 141 marks, glued to the word before ("waste.2") or after a space ("”. 3"); they are left as found, except in the first-words comparison.
- 16 paragraphs span a page break; paragraphs are 43 to 254 words of plain prose, no line ends with a hyphen; curly quotes and en dashes occur, so comparisons normalise them.

## The app, tab by tab

The arrangement of the workshop's Verbatim finder, with two tabs: a reader who sees such a tool for the first time needs the result and the paragraphs, and everything else stays one click away, closed.

**Header, always visible.** A monospace label "UN DOCUMENT · PDF TEXT", the serif `title`, one line: `symbol` linked to `doc_url` (new tab), "adopted `reference.adopted`", "n pages", `source`. At the right a green dot "n of m checks pass" or a red dot "n checks failed", then "n paragraphs flagged".

**Left rail, always visible.** Headed "DOCUMENT": a card with `symbol` in monospace and the short title. Two big serif numbers: "n paragraphs of `reference.paragraphs`" with a thin bar (red when short or over); "n paragraphs flagged" of the paragraphs found, in red when more than 0, "footnote text may sit inside: check them against the PDF". Then "n of m checks pass".

Under the header, numbered tabs (`role="tablist"`, arrow keys): `01 RESULT · 02 PARAGRAPHS`.

**01 RESULT. Did the app find everything the document has?** Four tiles, big serif numbers, a "How this is computed" line each: **Paragraphs found: n** beside **the document has `reference.paragraphs`** (green when equal, red with the difference); **First words match: n of `reference.paragraphs`**; **Paragraphs flagged: n of the paragraphs found**, on n pages, in red when more than 0, "footnote text may sit inside these paragraphs: check them against the PDF"; **Footnotes: not separated**, "the document has `reference.footnotes`; this version leaves them in place and flags them". When first words differ, the paragraphs concerned are listed under the tiles, one line each, "para. n: found … / reference …" (at most ten lines, then "and n more").

Under them **Take the paragraphs away**: {{q4}} The JSON file is an array of records, each with `symbol`, {{q1.export}}, `page_start`, `page_end`, `text`, `flagged`, `first_words_match`, `citation`, `doc_url` and `limitations` ("footnotes not separated; n may sit inside this paragraph" for a flagged paragraph, "footnotes not separated" for the others). The Markdown file opens with front matter between `---` lines (`title`, `symbol`, `adopted`, `source_url`, `extracted`: today's date, `paragraphs_found`, `paragraphs_expected`, `paragraphs_flagged`, `footnotes`: "not separated; the document has n"), then the headings as `##` and `###` lines in document order and each paragraph as its number in bold, then its text, with "(flagged: may contain footnote text)" after a flagged one. File names: the symbol with slashes replaced by hyphens; a Blob URL, UTF-8.

Last, two closed headings, buttons with `aria-expanded`: **Every check (m)**, the check panel described below, one line per check; and **Flagged paragraphs (n)**: {{q3}} Nothing else on the tab: at most seven things to click.

**02 PARAGRAPHS. What does each paragraph say, and how do I cite it?** {{q1}} Page: the page(s) it starts and ends on ("3–4" across a page break); First line: the first 120 characters cut at a word with "…"; Check: "OK", "first words differ" (red) or "may contain footnote text" (red). Rows are buttons with `aria-expanded`; click or Enter expands the row in place: the full text, verbatim as computed, never shortened, with suspect lines marked; the reference's six words beside the found six; {{q6}} {{q5}}

**Footer, always visible.** `source`, `built`, and "Done by this page's code; no model was called and nothing left the browser."

## How every number is computed

The pipeline runs once on load, in this order, over `records` sorted by `page`.

- **Header.** If a page's first non-empty line equals `symbol`, drop it; otherwise note a warning for that page.
- **Footer.** From the end of each page, drop lines while the line is empty, starts with "GE." (the job code), consists only of 6-digit groups (the date stamp), or is a bare number of one to three digits. A bare number equal to `page` is the page number; any other is counted as "bare number removed from the footer" (a footnote number the converter displaced; the app does not put it back).
- **Body lines of all pages are concatenated** (every line that is not header or footer, footnote lines included) in page order, each line tagged with its page; this joins the paragraphs that cross a page break.
- **Paragraph starts.** A line matching `/^(\d{1,3})\.$/` (number alone) or `/^(\d{1,3})\. (.+)$/` (number and text on one line; the text after the space is the first line). Lines before the first paragraph start are the cover.
- **Headings.** A line matching `/^([IVX]+|[A-Z])\.$/` opens a labelled heading: skip blank lines, then every line up to the next label line or paragraph start is heading text; a line starting with a lowercase letter or "(" continues the previous heading line. An **unlabelled heading** is a non-empty line immediately followed by a paragraph-start line, at most 90 characters, starting with a capital letter and not ending with a full stop, semicolon, colon, comma or digit; when the line before it passes the same test and does not end a paragraph sentence, the two lines are one heading. A heading line is never paragraph text. {{q1.compute}}
- **Paragraph lines.** Every other non-empty body line belongs to the current paragraph; blank lines are dropped. `page_start` and `page_end` are the pages of its first and last line.
{{q6.compute}}
- **Suspect lines.** A line inside a paragraph is suspect when it is a bare number of one to three digits with no full stop after it, or starts with one to three digits, a space and a capital letter, a UN document symbol or a quotation mark ("7 E/2003/22…", "2 Summary for policymakers…"), or starts with an asterisk and a space ("* Adopted by the Committee…", the note on the first page). A paragraph start always has a full stop after its number, so the two never mix. A suspect line and every line after it to the end of its page are suspect: a footnote block runs to the foot of the page. A paragraph over 300 words is flagged too (the longest real one here has 254). A paragraph is **flagged** when it has a suspect line or is over 300 words, and gets `flagged` true. On this file the rule flags 20 of 90 paragraphs, one per page: the paragraph that runs at the foot of each page, above its footnotes.
{{q3.compute}}
- **First words.** The first six whitespace-separated words of `text`, after removing footnote marks: digits glued to the end of a word or a punctuation mark are cut ("waste.2" becomes "waste."), and a token of digits alone is dropped only when the token before it ends with a full stop, comma or closing quote and is not an abbreviation such as "No." or "art." (paragraphs 24, 27, 46 and 60 start with real numbers, "article 2" or "No. 3", which must stay); compared with `reference.first_words[String(number)]`, equal after turning curly quotes straight, en and em dashes into a hyphen and runs of whitespace into one space; case is kept.
{{q5.compute}}
- **Counts** are loops in JavaScript; nothing is estimated, no model is called.

## How the app checks itself

Shown under **Every check** on tab 01, closed until opened. One line per check: what was compared, the two values, and "pass" in green or "check failed" in red with a link to the rows concerned. A failed check never hides a result.

- **Paragraph count.** Found against `reference.paragraphs`.
- **Numbering.** Exactly 1 to n in order; gaps and duplicates listed by number and page.
- **First words.** Mismatches counted; listed under the tiles of tab 01, the row flagged on tab 02.
- **Paragraphs flagged.** A flag is not a failure: the paragraph count can be right while footnote text sits inside a paragraph, so this line reads "n paragraphs flagged on n pages, to check against the PDF".
{{q3.checks}}
- **Headers and footers.** Pages whose first line was the symbol (expected all); pages with a page number in the footer (expected all but the first); bare numbers removed from the footer, listed with their page.
- **Headings.** The number of labelled and unlabelled headings, with the unlabelled ones listed, so a reader can spot a paragraph's last line mistaken for a heading.
- **Nothing lost.** Every non-empty line of every page is classified exactly once as cover, header, heading, paragraph or footer, and the counts per kind sum to the total non-empty lines in the file; any unclassified line is listed in red with its page.
- **Export round trip.** The JSON to download is parsed back; its record count equals the table's.

## Edge cases and risks

- A paragraph number on the same line as its text (2 of 90 here) and alone on its line (88) must both be accepted; handling one form only loses two paragraphs or finds none.
- "6 November 2025" on the cover starts with a number and a space; it is never suspect because the cover comes before the first paragraph.
- A line of real paragraph text may start with a number and a space ("17 Sustainable Development Goals"); it is flagged, which costs a reader one look at the PDF, never a lost line.
- The reference is a yardstick, not the truth: when the counts disagree, the app shows both and never trims or pads its result to match.
- If `reference` or one of its fields is missing, the tiles say "no reference in this file" and the checks that need it show "not run", never "pass"; if no paragraph is found, tab 01 says so and the exports are disabled.

## Design and accessibility

What this app adds to the studio look:

- **Red accent** on the active tab, the paragraph numbers, the flagged-paragraphs number and the words "first words differ", "may contain footnote text" and "check failed"; "pass" dark green: words as well as colours.
- **Big serif numbers** only on the rail and the tiles of tab 01. Every table has a serif `<caption>` stating the message ("90 paragraphs found, 90 expected"), a monospace number (`TAB.01`), `<th scope="col">`, numbers right-aligned.
- A suspect line in the expanded paragraph is marked by a thin red box.
- The check panel follows "Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code" (Analysis Function): each check tells a story, given this data, having run this code, we expect this output.
- The exports follow The Turing Way's "Documentation and metadata": a dataset travels with its source, its fields and its known limitations.
- Citations follow the Dag Hammarskjöld Library's "How should I cite a UN document?": fields stored apart and formatted on copy, the symbol as the key, the paragraph as the pinpoint.
- Keyboard: rows and closed headings are buttons with `aria-expanded`; a hidden tab panel is not focusable.

## Out of scope

No footnote separation: suspect lines are flagged and stay in the text. No model calls, no summaries, no OCR, no PDF rendering: the input is the converter's text. No editing in the browser, one document.

## Sources consulted

- The Turing Way, Documentation and metadata — https://github.com/the-turing-way/the-turing-way/blob/bcd8050eed319acc55f8ce0fe0410db157a17f04/book/website/reproducible-research/rdm/rdm-metadata.md
- UK Government Analysis Function, Quality assurance of code for analysis and research: Testing code — https://github.com/best-practice-and-impact/qa-of-code-guidance/blob/fa39f2089905fe07c08ae4d66671736a1becd3c5/book/testing_code.md
- Dag Hammarskjöld Library, Ask DAG: how should I cite a UN document? — https://ask.un.org/faq/401380
